source.title: Data Doping or True Intelligence? Evaluating the Transferability of Injected Knowledge in LLMs
source.authors: Essa Jan; Moiz Ali; M. Hassan; Fareed Zaffar; Yasir Zaki

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling questions to knowledge retention after supervised fine-tuning on injected facts, rather than testing pretraining loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports accuracy after fine-tuning at four Qwen2.5 sizes, which bears on retention scaling in a fine-tuning setting. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit a power law, or test a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. The generic-question results are not reported by model size in a table.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes four Qwen2.5 sizes (1.5B–72B) on injected facts and reports direct-question accuracy by size, so its own results bear on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6) in a fine-tuning knowledge-injection setting. It reports no loss, no power-law fit and no compute or allocation analysis, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that retention scales with model size and that task format strongly affects retention, with application in broader contexts still limited. Their statement that knowledge integration follows a power law is asserted, not fitted.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes models on injected facts and measures factual-answer accuracy; it does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Retention results vary with fine-tuning format (QA, blanks, translation, text-to-JSON) and evaluation type (direct versus generic questions). The size sweep is limited to Qwen2.5.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The scaling comparison is limited to one model family and four sizes. No power-law fit, exponents, prediction test, or uncertainty estimates are reported. The generic-question results are not tabulated by model size.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's cross-architecture task-format results and Table 2's generic-question results were not extracted because they do not provide a size sweep; Appendix B's pre-fine-tuning baseline table was omitted because it is not a post-injection scaling comparison.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No allocation of a fixed compute budget between parameters and tokens.
No variation of shape at a fixed parameter count.
No loss is measured and no power-law form is fitted for the fine-tuning setting; four accuracy points cannot establish the form.

Predictability (a fitted trend, or prediction from pretraining loss) is not tested. Standard benchmarks and model families other than Qwen2.5 are not tested. Size is confounded with each checkpoint's distinct pretraining.
No comparison of fitting choices and no test of curvature.

missing.what: Generic-question accuracy by Qwen2.5 size. The text says larger models improve on generic questions but stay much lower; no per-size numbers are given.
Pre-fine-tuning baselines for the Qwen2.5 sizes (3B 8%, 32B 15%, 72B 15%); needed as row baselines.

record.verdict_notes: This is weak evidence on scaling: four sizes from one family, no uncertainty, and a GPT-4o-mini judge (94% agreement with humans). It does not separate model size from pretraining differences. The 1.5B→3B translation gain is only 1 point.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute is not measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and training tokens is evaluated.
Depth, width, and architecture variations at fixed parameter count are not tested.
The study evaluates injected-knowledge retention after SFT for Qwen2.5 at four sizes, but does not fit or establish a power-law form or test other modalities, repeated data, or transfer.
It measures accuracy on custom direct and generic factual questions after knowledge-injection fine-tuning, but does not test standard downstream benchmarks or relate performance to pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, or training schedules, nor test whether fitted curves bend away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B/32B/72B fine-tuned on QA, translation, blank or JSON formats; direct-question accuracy
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically with size in all four formats, e.g. QA 38%→72% (r1–r4) and JSON 20%→39% (r13–r16). Gains also exceed the pre-fine-tuning baselines of 8–15%.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased at every tested size in all four formats, including 38% to 72% for QA and 20% to 39% for JSON, exceeding pre-fine-tuning baselines of 8–15%.
